## Required Packages

```{r packages, message = FALSE}
library(NNS)
library(prophet)
packageVersion("NNS")
packageVersion("prophet")
```

## Comparison Design

Each comparison gives both methods the same training data and forecast origin
and scores the same horizon. Neither method is tuned on the test window:
`prophet` runs with its default settings, and `NNS.ARMA` uses either calendar
lags fixed in advance or the periods `NNS.seas` finds in the training data. A
last-value forecast is scored alongside as a reference.

The archived page (November 2017) differed in three ways. It chose the Peyton
Manning periods with the lowest error on the test year, which made that year
part of the tuning; its lynx `prophet` forecast had 35 values for 34 test years;
and its S&P 500 data came from Yahoo Finance, which this build cannot
download. Its scores and tallies are not carried forward.

```{r helpers}
rmse <- function(f, a) sqrt(mean((f - a)^2))
# Download a file once per build and check it is the version this page used.
fetch <- function(url, md5) {
  path <- file.path(tempdir(), basename(url))
  if (!file.exists(path)) download.file(url, path, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
  stopifnot(unname(tools::md5sum(path)) == md5)
  path
}
results <- list()
record <- function(name, h, prophet_fc, nns_fc, actual, last_value, seconds) {
  results[[name]] <<- data.frame(Comparison = name, Horizon = h,
                                 `prophet RMSE` = rmse(prophet_fc, actual),
                                 `NNS RMSE` = rmse(nns_fc, actual),
                                 `Last value RMSE` = rmse(last_value, actual),
                                 `prophet s` = seconds[1], `NNS s` = seconds[2],
                                 check.names = FALSE)
  results[[name]][, 3:5]
}
timed <- function(expr) {
  t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
  value <- expr
  list(value = value, seconds = proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0)
}
```

## Retail Sales Example

Below is the retail sales data incorporated with the Facebook `prophet`
repository.

```{r retail-data}
retail <- read.csv(fetch(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/facebook/prophet/main/examples/example_retail_sales.csv",
  "efbd7c178abf498e5db39eb1ff3c84a3"))
retail$ds <- as.Date(retail$ds)
range(retail$ds)
```

We are forecasting the last 50 periods...

```{r retail-split}
l <- length(retail[, 1]) - 50
```

### prophet model:

```{r retail-prophet}
p <- timed({
  m <- prophet(retail[1:l, ])
  predict(m, data.frame(ds = retail$ds[(l + 1):nrow(retail)]))
})
retail_fcst <- p$value
plot(m, predict(m, data.frame(ds = retail$ds)))
```

### NNS model:

`NNS` uses the 12-month calendar lag and a linear regression of each lag's
components.

```{r retail-nns}
n <- timed(NNS.ARMA(retail[, 2], h = 50, seasonal.factor = 12, method = 'lin',
                    training.set = l, seasonal.plot = FALSE))
nns.retail.fcst <- n$value
```

### MSE:

```{r retail-mse}
c(prophet = mean((retail_fcst$yhat - tail(retail[, 2], 50))^2),
  NNS = mean((nns.retail.fcst - tail(retail[, 2], 50))^2))
record("Retail sales", 50, retail_fcst$yhat, nns.retail.fcst, tail(retail[, 2], 50),
       retail[l, 2], c(p$seconds, n$seconds))
```

## Peyton Manning Example (Raw Values)

Next is the Peyton Manning example from the Facebook `prophet` repository:
daily log page views of Peyton Manning's Wikipedia page. The repository now
ships only the log file; the raw views are its exponent. Twenty-nine days are
missing, so `NNS.ARMA`'s lags count observations rather than calendar days,
while `prophet` uses the dates.

```{r pm-data}
log_omaha <- read.csv(fetch(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/facebook/prophet/main/examples/example_wp_log_peyton_manning.csv",
  "43a15e3f903a6e82cc0a53f0be249575"))
log_omaha$ds <- as.Date(log_omaha$ds)
omaha <- data.frame(ds = log_omaha$ds, y = exp(log_omaha$y))
range(omaha$ds)
sum(diff(omaha$ds) > 1)
```

We are forecasting the last 365 periods...

```{r pm-split}
l <- length(omaha[, 1]) - 365
test_days <- omaha$ds[(l + 1):nrow(omaha)]
```

### prophet model:

```{r pm-prophet}
p <- timed({
  m <- prophet(omaha[1:l, ])
  predict(m, data.frame(ds = test_days))
})
omaha_fcst <- p$value
plot(m, predict(m, data.frame(ds = omaha$ds)))
```

### NNS model:

`NNS` is using a `seasonal.factor = c(1, sf)`, which translates to a daily and
the best reported lag from our seasonality test on the training data. This is
not optimized.

```{r pm-nns}
sf <- NNS.seas(omaha[1:l, 2], plot = FALSE)$best.period
sf
n <- timed(NNS.ARMA(omaha[, 2], h = 365, seasonal.factor = c(1, sf), method = 'lin',
                    training.set = l, seasonal.plot = FALSE))
nns.omaha.fcst <- n$value
```

### MSE:

```{r pm-mse}
c(prophet = mean((omaha_fcst$yhat - tail(omaha[, 2], 365))^2),
  NNS = mean((nns.omaha.fcst - tail(omaha[, 2], 365))^2))
record("Peyton Manning, raw", 365, omaha_fcst$yhat, nns.omaha.fcst, tail(omaha[, 2], 365),
       omaha[l, 2], c(p$seconds, n$seconds))
```

## Peyton Manning Example (Log Values)

Using the log values of the preceding Peyton Manning dataset. Again, we are
forecasting the last 365 periods...

### prophet model:

```{r pm-log-prophet}
p <- timed({
  m <- prophet(log_omaha[1:l, ])
  predict(m, data.frame(ds = test_days))
})
log_omaha_fcst <- p$value
plot(m, predict(m, data.frame(ds = log_omaha$ds)))
```

### NNS model:

```{r pm-log-nns}
sf <- NNS.seas(log_omaha[1:l, 2], plot = FALSE)$best.period
sf
n <- timed(NNS.ARMA(log_omaha[, 2], h = 365, seasonal.factor = c(1, sf), method = 'nonlin',
                    training.set = l, seasonal.plot = FALSE))
nns.log.omaha.fcst <- n$value
```

### MSE:

```{r pm-log-mse}
c(prophet = mean((log_omaha_fcst$yhat - tail(log_omaha[, 2], 365))^2),
  NNS = mean((nns.log.omaha.fcst - tail(log_omaha[, 2], 365))^2))
record("Peyton Manning, log", 365, log_omaha_fcst$yhat, nns.log.omaha.fcst,
       tail(log_omaha[, 2], 365), log_omaha[l, 2], c(p$seconds, n$seconds))
```

### Notes

Can we recover better raw estimates from translated log estimates for
`prophet`, or better log estimates from translated raw estimates for `NNS`?
The exponent of a log forecast is a median-type forecast of the raw views, not
their mean.

```{r pm-translate}
c(`prophet, exp(log forecast) vs raw` = mean((exp(log_omaha_fcst$yhat) - tail(omaha[, 2], 365))^2),
  `prophet, raw forecast vs raw` = mean((omaha_fcst$yhat - tail(omaha[, 2], 365))^2))
c(`NNS, log(raw forecast) vs log` = mean((log(nns.omaha.fcst) - tail(log_omaha[, 2], 365))^2),
  `NNS, log forecast vs log` = mean((nns.log.omaha.fcst - tail(log_omaha[, 2], 365))^2))
```

## lynx Dataset

Next we test the Canadian lynx dataset suggested from Andrew Gelman's blog post
on prophet: <http://andrewgelman.com/2017/03/01/facebooks-prophet-uses-stan/>.
The annual trappings from 1821 to 1934 are split into the first 80 years for
training and the last 34 for testing.

```{r lynx-data}
data(lynx)
l <- length(lynx) - 34
lynx_df <- data.frame(ds = as.Date(paste0(time(lynx), "-01-01")), y = as.numeric(lynx))
```

### prophet model and RMSE:

```{r lynx-prophet}
p <- timed({
  m <- prophet(lynx_df[1:l, ])
  predict(m, data.frame(ds = lynx_df$ds[(l + 1):nrow(lynx_df)]))
})
fcast <- p$value
sqrt(mean((tail(lynx, 34) - fcast$yhat)^2))
plot(m, predict(m, data.frame(ds = lynx_df$ds)))
```

### NNS model and RMSE:

`NNS` uses the two best periods `NNS.seas` finds in the 80 training years.

```{r lynx-nns}
n <- timed(NNS.ARMA(lynx, h = 34, training.set = l, method = 'lin', seasonal.factor = FALSE,
                    best.periods = 2, seasonal.plot = FALSE))
nns.lynx <- n$value
sqrt(mean((nns.lynx - tail(lynx, 34))^2))
record("lynx", 34, fcast$yhat, nns.lynx, tail(lynx, 34), lynx[l], c(p$seconds, n$seconds))
```

## S&P 500

Finally we are going to forecast 252 trading days of the S&P 500 index, at
three consecutive forecast origins. The archived page used SPY prices from
2007 to 2017 downloaded from Yahoo Finance with `quantmod`. This build uses
FRED's `SP500` series (index closes from S&P Dow Jones Indices), downloaded at
build time; FRED keeps the most recent ten years. Each origin is trained on the
1260 trading days (about five years) before it, so the windows stay inside
FRED's range when the page is rebuilt, until late 2028.

```{r sp-data}
sp <- read.csv("https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=SP500", na.strings = ".")
sp <- sp[!is.na(sp[[2]]), ]
sp <- data.frame(ds = as.Date(sp[[1]]), y = sp[[2]])
sp <- sp[sp$ds <= as.Date("2026-10-30"), ]
origins <- nrow(sp) - 252 * (3:1)
data.frame(Year = 1:3,
           `Training from` = sp$ds[origins - 1259], `Origin` = sp$ds[origins],
           `Test from` = sp$ds[origins + 1], `Test to` = sp$ds[origins + 252],
           check.names = FALSE)
```

`NNS` is using a `seasonal.factor = c(1, 5, 21, 63, 126, 252)`, which
translates to a daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly, bi-annual and annual lag
for S&P closing prices.

```{r sp-forecasts, fig.height = 9}
par(mfrow = c(3, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (k in 1:3) {
  window <- (origins[k] - 1259):(origins[k] + 252)
  train <- sp[window[1:1260], ]
  test <- sp[window[1261:1512], ]
  p <- timed({
    m <- prophet(train)
    predict(m, data.frame(ds = test$ds))
  })
  n <- timed(NNS.ARMA(train$y, h = 252, seasonal.factor = c(1, 5, 21, 63, 126, 252),
                      method = 'nonlin', plot = FALSE, seasonal.plot = FALSE))
  print(record(paste0("S&P 500, year ", k), 252, p$value$yhat, n$value, test$y,
               tail(train$y, 1), c(p$seconds, n$seconds)))
  plot(c(train$ds, test$ds), c(train$y, test$y), type = "l", xlab = "", ylab = "S&P 500",
       main = paste0("Year ", k, ": ", test$ds[1], " to ", test$ds[252]))
  lines(test$ds, p$value$yhat, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
  lines(test$ds, n$value, col = "red", lwd = 2)
  abline(v = train$ds[1260], lty = 3)
  legend("topleft", legend = c("Actual", "prophet", "NNS"), col = c("black", "blue", "red"),
         lty = 1, lwd = c(1, 2, 2), bty = "n")
}
```

## Summary

```{r summary}
summary_table <- do.call(rbind, results)
knitr::kable(summary_table, digits = c(0, 0, 4, 4, 4, 1, 1), row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Test RMSE and run time (seconds) of each forecast")
```

```{r summary-counts, include = FALSE}
nns_lower <- sum(summary_table[["NNS RMSE"]] < summary_table[["prophet RMSE"]])
naive_vs_prophet <- sum(summary_table[["Last value RMSE"]] < summary_table[["prophet RMSE"]])
naive_vs_nns <- sum(summary_table[["Last value RMSE"]] < summary_table[["NNS RMSE"]])
secs <- function(x) paste(sprintf("%.1f", range(x)), collapse = " to ")
```

`NNS.ARMA` has the lower RMSE in `r nns_lower` of these `r nrow(summary_table)`
forecasts and `prophet` in `r nrow(summary_table) - nns_lower`. The last-value
forecast is more accurate than `prophet` in `r naive_vs_prophet` and than
`NNS.ARMA` in `r naive_vs_nns`. Each `prophet` fit took
`r secs(summary_table[["prophet s"]])` seconds here and each `NNS.ARMA` forecast
`r secs(summary_table[["NNS s"]])` seconds.

These are single forecast origins for retail sales, Peyton Manning (raw and
log) and lynx, and three consecutive years of the S&P 500, so they describe
these windows rather than rank the methods. A ranking would need many origins
per series, scored with the same data, origins, horizon and tuning budget for
every method.

To be fair, `prophet` was not altered from its default settings and any
interested readers are more than welcome to suggest different settings to
improve performance. `NNS` was not optimized either.

> **Note (2026).** The archived page's scores, including the running tally,
> came from test-window period selection (Peyton Manning), a misaligned lynx
> comparison and SPY data that cannot be reproduced; they are withdrawn. See
> `examples/example-corrections.md`.
